summary: Defines a new mail header, Message-Context, based on RFC 2822, that gives information about the context and presentation of a message. A receiving mail client may use it as a hint for how best to present the message, for example as voice mail or fax.

plainLanguage.summary: Message-Context is an email header that says what kind of message the sender intends, such as voice mail or fax. A receiving mail program may use it to choose how to present the message, but it must remain only a hint.

questions: how does a mail client use message-context
subtitle: A message-level header that hints whether an email is voice mail, fax, paging, or text.

tldr.problem: A mail client may not be able to infer whether a message is voice mail, fax, paging, or ordinary email from its body parts alone.
tldr.mechanism: The sender can add a top-level Message-Context header with a registered class, which a receiving user agent may use as a hint for presentation.
tldr.outcome: The value is only a hint; a receiver must still present content properly when the header is missing or wrong. RFC 3458 was updated by RFC 3938.

today: RFC 3458 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2003 and was updated by RFC 3938.

sections.title: A Message-Level Context Header
sections.content:
RFC 3458 defines the Message-Context header to describe how a recipient is expected to interact with a message. Examples include email, voice mail, and fax.

A receiving user agent may use this information to select a viewer, choose an icon, arrange an inbox, or filter messages. Unlike Content-Disposition, which gives a presentation hint for one body part, Message-Context describes the message as a whole.
sections.plainLanguage: This header identifies the intended context of a whole message. A mail program can use it to choose an icon or presentation method.

sections.title: Why Message Content Is Not Enough
sections.content:
The media types inside a message do not always reveal the sender's intent. Audio and image parts might be a fax with voice commentary, a voice message with diagrams, or an aggregate multimedia message.

Two messages may use the same media type but serve different purposes, such as traditional email and an SMS message. A user agent that scans every body part to infer intent may also need to inspect large voice or video objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Media types show what data a message contains, but not always what the sender means by it. A separate header can state that context without scanning the body.

sections.title: A Header That Remains a Hint
sections.content:
The RFC chose a top-level message header because context applies to the message as a whole. It does not require a user agent to support any particular content, and it does not request a delivery notification.

A receiving user agent MUST NOT rely on the value in a way that prevents proper presentation. If the value is wrong or does not match the body, the message must still be presented at least as meaningfully as if the header were absent.

The header may affect whether or where a user agent displays a message, but it should not change how the content itself is rendered.
sections.plainLanguage: The context value can guide where or when a message appears, but it cannot control whether the content is displayed correctly. A wrong value must not make the message fail.

sections.title: The Header and Its Initial Classes
sections.content:
The field has the form Message-Context: message-context-class. The header name and class value are case-insensitive, and class values must be registered with IANA.

The initial classes are voice-message, fax-message, pager-message, multimedia-message, text-message, and none. The header may appear zero or one times in a message.

If the header is absent, the receiving user agent MUST handle the message as though its value were none.
sections.plainLanguage: The header can name voice mail, fax, paging, multimedia, text email, or no context. If it is missing, the receiver treats the context as none.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Message-Context is not proof that a message is safe or that its contents match the label. A poorly designed user agent must not execute a mailed program just because a context label says to do so.

A misleading context value could also cause unwanted processing or contribute to denial of service. The RFC therefore requires receivers to treat the value as a hint only.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender can provide a misleading context value. A mail program must not treat the label as permission to execute content or bypass normal presentation.

sections.title: Registering New Context Classes
sections.content:
IANA maintains the Internet Message Context Types registry with a Specification Required policy. A new context class requires a published RFC that includes the registration template and describes interoperability and security issues.

The template asks for a class name, a short description, and contact information. This process gives different user agents a shared meaning for each registered value.
sections.plainLanguage: New context labels must be registered through a published specification. The registry gives user agents a shared definition for each class.
